notes: Actual results for calendar year 2025, as the county reported them in its annual report to the Washington State Auditor. Not a budget.
Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included.
Spending is reported by function (BARS account) for every fund, utilities included; capital expenditures count under their function when paid.

Internal service funds (equipment rental, self-insurance, information technology and the like; $175,208,182 of their revenue and spending) are left out, since the departments they serve report that spending.
Borrowing, transfers between funds, interfund loans, refunded debt and depreciation are left out.
General government, courts, legal services, planning, economic development, housing and conservation count as overhead.

Political money counts cash contributions from businesses, unions and PACs to county commissioner, council, executive, sheriff, prosecutor and other county office candidates, reported to the Public Disclosure Commission since 2023. Washington allows business and union contributions to local candidates. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and caucus committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-18. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for Washington yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

Debt outstanding: $268,616,000 (long-term plus short-term debt at the end of the fiscal year ending 2024-12-31), as Spokane County reported it to the U.S. Census Bureau's 2024 Annual Survey of Local Government Finances. The state's own data does not report debt. That is a different year from the revenue and spending shown (FY 2025).

redFlags.label: Video analytics
redFlags.detail: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office uses Briefcam video analytics software.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS011930, citing Crosscut

redFlags.label: Real-time crime center
redFlags.detail: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office began operating a real-time crime center in 2023.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS011896, citing The Spokesman

redFlags.label: Private camera registry
redFlags.detail: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office has a voluntary camera registry program.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS007593, citing KHQ

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office Regional Air Support Unit operates two DJI drones as of 2018, according to data compiled by the Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS003870, citing Center for the Study of the Drone at Bard College

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: As of April 2024, the Spokane County Sheriff's Office operates 39 Flock Safety automated license plate readers. The agency stores ALPR data for 30 days.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS011908, citing Flock Safety

redFlags.label: Third-party investigative platform
redFlags.detail: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office has used Coplink X, which has been renamed CrimeTracer.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS013252, citing SoundThinking
